title: NASA's ERNEST Rover Drives Itself 16 Miles, Paving the Way for Smarter Space Exploration
summary: A four-wheeled robot named ERNEST just aced a grueling road trip—and it didn't need a driver. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) recently sent the Exploration Rover for Navigating Extreme Sloped Terrain (ERNEST) on a 16-mile (26-kilometer) journey through Southern California's desert. Over seven days and 37 hours of driving, the rover navigated almost entirely on its own, with minimal human intervention. That's a dramatic leap from current Mars rovers: Perseverance, after five years on the Red Planet, has only just covered a marathon's distance. ERNEST's secret lies in its innovative hardware and adaptive artificial intelligence. Unlike traditional rovers with a passive rocker-bogie suspension, ERNEST uses an active system with gimballing joints on its front chassis. This allows it to alter its gait, mimicking squirming, wheel-walking, and climbing motions. Each wheel can also steer independently, enabling sideways maneuvers. The rover's AI was trained through reinforcement learning in a virtual environment, racking up thousands of hours of simulated experience in just days. After proving itself in JPL's Mars Yard, it graduated to the desert. During the test, ERNEST handled poor lighting and nighttime driving—conditions meant to mimic the moon's harsh shadows. The 4-foot-long rover cruised at up to 0.6 mph, already faster than current off-world rovers. Engineers envision scaling up the technology for larger rovers that can travel farther and faster, accessing steep craters and shadowed regions that have been off-limits. Issa Nesnas, a JPL principal technologist, said the testing refines both mobility hardware and autonomy software for extreme lunar distances. With ERNEST, the future of planetary exploration looks not just autonomous, but unstoppable.
why_it_matters: Autonomous rovers like ERNEST could one day explore places too dangerous for humans, like lava tubes on the Moon or steep cliffs on Mars, searching for water ice or signs of life. This technology also feeds into the future of self-driving cars on Earth, where similar AI must handle unpredictable terrain.

background_read: NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Pasadena, California, has designed every Mars rover, from the tiny Sojourner in 1997 to the SUV-sized Perseverance, which landed in Jezero Crater in 2021. Perseverance's main mission is to collect rock samples that will one day be returned to Earth.

For decades, rover suspension has relied on the passive rocker-bogie system, which uses a linkage of arms to keep all six wheels in contact with uneven ground without springs – a design first proven on Sojourner.

True autonomy for off-world driving is extremely difficult because radio signals to Mars take between 4 and 24 minutes one-way, so a rover must analyze terrain and make navigation decisions instantly without waiting for human commands.
JPL's Mars Yard is a dusty outdoor testing ground that mimics Martian rock fields and slopes, allowing engineers to rehearse maneuvers before sending commands to the real rover on another planet.

The ERNEST rover's 16-mile desert drive is longer than the total distance covered by the Perseverance rover on Mars in five years, highlighting how autonomy and better mobility can transform exploration.

perspectives.description: Roboticists see ERNEST as a huge leap forward. An active suspension that lets a rover squirm and climb means access to steep craters and shadowed regions never before reached. This kind of autonomy could double the distance future missions cover, multiplying scientific returns.

Some warn that relying heavily on AI-driven rovers raises the stakes: a software glitch or an unexpected terrain trap could strand the robot far from base, wasting years of work. Others argue that focusing too much on autonomous robots might take funding away from human exploration, which inspires more public support.

The shift from passive rocker-bogie to active joints mimics how animals like crabs or insects adapt to rough ground. This convergence of biology and robotics illustrates a trend where engineers look to nature for solutions, potentially making future rovers as agile as living creatures.

Translating ERNEST's success to the Moon or Mars will be difficult. Extreme temperatures, abrasive dust, and radiation can damage delicate actuators and sensors. Engineers will need lighter, tougher materials and even smarter software that can handle 100-mile traverses without human check-ins. The next step is to ruggedize the design and test it in even harsher environments.
